concurrency_mechanism: CeleryExecutor. Three caps were aligned on 20 so exactly one of them binds at 20 and none binds lower: core.parallelism=20 (deployment-wide), core.max_active_tasks_per_dag=20 (per DAG) and celery.worker_concurrency=20 (prefork pool size on the single airflow-worker container). default_pool keeps its 128 slots, so pool slots never bind. The Celery prefork pool forks one OS process per task instance, so CPU-bound task bodies get real cores.

core.parallelism.why: hard cap on concurrently running task instances across the whole deployment

core.max_active_tasks_per_dag.why: per-DAG cap; the default 16 would have bound below 20

celery.worker_concurrency.why: Celery prefork pool size on the single worker container; the default 16 would have bound below 20

core.max_map_length.why: dynamic task mapping refuses to expand past this; 2000 inputs need it raised

core.load_examples.why: left on: 'stock' is defined as the official compose, which ships 115 example DAGs loaded and re-parsed

scheduler.max_tis_per_query.why: left at default; measured enqueue batches averaged 9.0, so this cap was never reached

core.default_pool_task_slot_count.why: default_pool has 128 slots, well above 20, so pool slots never bound

AIRFLOW_UID.why: the step the official docker-compose guide requires on Linux so the mounted dags/ and logs/ are writable; not a tuning

notes: Fan-out: one DAG (tp_sleep), one @task mapped with .expand() over a literal list of 2000 ints, so all 2000 task instances belong to a single DAG run. They are created up-front: in every rep max(scheduled_dttm) was at or before min(start_date), i.e. all 2000 were in 'scheduled' state before the first one started, so submission is not the bottleneck (the harness also saw all 2000 rows on its first poll, <1s after the trigger). Example DAGs were left ENABLED because 'stock' is defined as the official compose unchanged; the DB held 117 DAGs (115 examples + 2 benchmark). Peak concurrency was exactly 20 in every rep and never exceeded it, but time-weighted mean concurrency was only 7.2 of 20: Airflow did not sustain 20-way concurrency. The scheduler moved task instances to 'queued' in ~227 bursts per run averaging 8.8 task instances (max 20), roughly 1.7 bursts/s, with a median 0.41s gap between enqueue instants, so the 20 worker slots sat partly idle between bursts. scheduler.max_tis_per_query (default 16) was never reached. Timings read from task_instance.queued_dttm / start_date / end_date.
measurement: All reported numbers are derived from the Airflow metadata DB (task_instance), not harness wall-clock. throughput = n_success / (max(end_date) - min(start_date)). latency = end_date - queued_dttm. exec = end_date - start_date. Peak and mean concurrency are a sweep line over the (start_date, end_date) intervals. mean_busy_cores_host comes from an independent 1Hz /proc/stat sampler on the host (32 cores, nothing else running).
fanout: single DAG run; one @task mapped with .expand() over a literal list of 2000 inputs (dynamic task mapping), giving 2000 independent task instances
theoretical_ceiling_basis: 20 concurrent / 0.100 (time.sleep(0.1)) s of work per task
